sections.label: Introduction — The Opportunity We Are Missing
sections.title: The Opportunity We Are Missing

runs.text: Consider a procurement lead at a mid-sized manufacturer. Call her Meera. Two years ago, comparing four packaging suppliers took her most of a week: reading proposals, building a cost model, checking delivery records. Last month she did it in an afternoon. An AI assistant extracted the terms, built the comparison table and drafted a recommendation. The document looked better than anything she had produced before.

In the review meeting, the finance head asked two questions. Why does the recommended supplier look cheaper over three years when its unit price is higher? Meera answered well; she had checked the freight assumptions herself. Then: what happens to this choice if the new plant opens six months late? She paused. The model had assumed an opening date she had never questioned, and she could not say how much the recommendation depended on it.

Nothing went wrong that day. The question was noted and the decision deferred by a week. I keep returning to that pause all the same. The memo was better than anything Meera had written before, yet her grasp of what it rested on was, in one important place, thinner than the document suggested. A well-argued memo has never been conclusive evidence of its author's understanding; people have always had help from colleagues and editors. But AI makes it possible to produce sophisticated work with remarkably little understanding of the subject, and so the distinction between what we can produce and what we actually understand matters more than it used to. AI is plainly expanding what we can accomplish. Is it expanding what we are capable of understanding? That second question is far less settled, and it is the one this book is about.
I call the space between those two things the
intellectual capability gap

: the distance between what a person can produce with assistance and what they can independently explain, evaluate, transfer to a new situation or responsibly decide. I mean it as a way of looking at work, not as a score, and there is nothing shameful about using tools. Calculators, spreadsheets and search engines all let people produce work they could not do unaided, and that is usually good. The gap matters when you are the one who must
defend the work, adapt it when conditions change or take responsibility for what follows.

runs.text: The gap is not destiny, and this is where I part company with much of the current conversation. Most writing about AI and thinking is defensive: how do we stop our skills eroding? It is a fair question, but a small one. The larger question is what people could become if they treated the time and effort AI saves as raw material for growth. Generations of professionals have wished for more time to think. Many of us now have a little of it, and we are spending it, mostly without noticing, on more output.
My argument is that the gap can be narrowed from the other side. Most of us now save some time and effort through AI. I call that saving the
intellectual dividend of AI

because, like any dividend, it can be spent, kept or reinvested. More output, more rest and more learning are all legitimate uses of it. What I propose is that some of it, regularly and on purpose, should go to the last of these: to learning, reflection, reasoning and exploration. I call that choice
cognitive reinvestment

. It guarantees nothing. Much depends on how the time is used and on the conditions in which we work, and if your saved time is seldom yours to direct, Chapter 2 offers small practices that fit inside the work itself.

Before deciding how to invest in our own development, though, we need to be clear about something in the nature of thinking itself. Knowing something, understanding it and exercising judgment about it are three different capabilities, and AI touches each of them differently. Chapter 1 begins there. Much later, in Chapter 9, the argument turns into a habit for single pieces of AI-assisted work, which I call
Think, Consult, Challenge, Verify, Own
. I have come to see that habit as reinvestment on a small scale, one task at a time.

None of this comes from nowhere. Research on cognitive offloading, deliberate practice, metacognition and human–AI collaboration, cited in later chapters, supplies most of the ingredients. Workplace advice to "reinvest the time AI saves" is common too, though it usually means reinvesting in more or better output. What I add is a claim and a practice: that the time AI saves should be judged partly by what it does to the person who saved it, and a way of acting on that judgment week by week.

AI tools will change many times before your career ends, and a book about any particular tool would date within months. This one is about capabilities that keep their value however the tools evolve: telling information from understanding, testing assumptions, reaching and revising your own conclusions, connecting ideas across fields, reasoning about systems and uncertainty, weighing objectives that conflict, and using AI without handing over your accountability. I hope you finish with a routine as well as some ideas, and with something harder to measure: a conviction that becoming a better thinker is worth doing for its own sake, whatever the job market happens to ask.
Readers who know Daniel Kahneman's
Thinking, Fast and Slow
, Julia Galef's
The Scout Mindset
, David Epstein's
Range
, Donella Meadows's
Thinking in Systems
, Nicholas Carr's
The Glass Cage
, Cal Newport's
Deep Work
or Ethan Mollick's
Co-Intelligence

will meet familiar ideas here, and I draw on several of them gladly. Carr warned more than a decade ago that automation can erode the very skills it relieves us of. Newport argued that the ability to concentrate on demanding work is becoming rarer just as it becomes more valuable. This book starts where those arguments leave off. It asks less how to protect ourselves from capable machines, or how to work alongside them, than what we might deliberately become with the time and effort they give back. The synthesis and its practical application are mine; the underlying concepts belong to the people cited.

A few suggestions on reading. Each chapter ends with an exercise and a reflective question. Do the exercises with your own work, not imagined cases; they take fifteen to thirty minutes and they are where most of the value lies. Question what you read here, including the frameworks. I have tried to keep five kinds of claim distinct: established findings; emerging evidence, such as preprints and single studies; conceptual research; philosophical reasoning; and my own propositions, which I mark with phrases such as “my argument” or “I propose”. Where the evidence is limited, I say so, and you should hold me to that standard. And come back to your answers after a few weeks, to see which of them you would still defend.
If I had to put the book's argument in a single sentence, it would be this:
the purpose of cognitive reinvestment is to ensure that as the intelligence available to us grows, the intellectual capability within us grows too.
Start, then, with an old distinction that AI has made urgent again: having access to knowledge is not the same as having it.

sections.title: Rethinking Human Value

sections.label: Chapter 1 — When Knowledge Is No Longer Enough
sections.title: When Knowledge Is No Longer Enough

runs.text: A first-year analyst and a thirty-year veteran can now open the same AI assistant and receive the same fluent analysis. Sophisticated intellectual help is far easier to come by than it was even a few years ago, but the ability to reason without it still has to be practised. Whether either of them can see the gaps in that analysis, test its claims or act on it wisely depends on what each has built through their own work and study. That difference, and what it does to the value of knowing things, is where I want to start.

Two regional sales managers at a consumer-goods company receive the same AI-generated analysis on a Monday morning. Sales in their regions have fallen for two quarters. The analysis is clear and well organised. It attributes the decline to a competitor's price cuts and recommends a targeted discount.

The first manager, Rahul, reads it, finds it persuasive and forwards it to his team with a plan to launch the discount. The second, Anita, reads the same document and stops at one line. The analysis treats all customers as one group. She knows that in her region a large share of revenue comes from small neighbourhood stores, and that several distributors serving those stores changed their credit terms recently. The competitor's price cut is real. But is it the cause?

Anita spends two hours checking. She may find that the analysis was right. She may find a different story. Neither scrutiny nor acceptance guarantees a good outcome; Rahul's discount might work perfectly well. What separates them is capability, more than personality or diligence. Anita knew enough about her market to notice what the analysis left out, and she knew how to test a causal claim rather than accept one.
From scarce information to scarce understanding

For much of professional history, information was hard to get. Knowing the regulations, the market data or the technical standard gave you an advantage because others had to search for it. In many settings that is less true today. Search engines and AI systems retrieve, organise and summarise information quickly.
The shift is uneven. Information quality varies, access is not universal, and much valuable knowledge — how your customers

actually behave, what your organisation tried last year — is not written down anywhere an AI can reach. Still, for a large range of professional questions, getting an answer is no longer the hard part. Knowing whether the answer is right, why it is right and what to do about it remains hard.
Three kinds of intellectual work are worth pulling apart here.

rows: Verify material facts; retain essential domain knowledge
Test causes, assumptions, context and alternatives
Choose objectives, weigh consequences, own the decision

runs.text: AI can contribute at every level. It is not always most reliable at retrieving facts, and it is not incapable of useful reasoning about decisions. Reliability depends on the task and the context. The table describes where
your
responsibility sits, not where AI stops.
Working through a falling-sales problem

Return to Anita's region. At the knowledge level, her first question is whether the decline is real and how large it is. Is it in volume or in value? Is it across all products or concentrated in a few? A reporting change or a stock adjustment can create an apparent decline that customers never caused.

At the understanding level, she asks why. The competitor's discount is one explanation. Changed distributor credit terms are another. A third might be a shift in what small stores choose to stock. Each explanation predicts something different. If price is the cause, the decline should be sharpest where the competitor is present. If credit terms are the cause, it should be sharpest among stores served by the affected distributors. She can check those patterns.

At the judgment level, she decides what to do. Even if credit terms turn out to be the main cause, there are several possible responses: support distributors, change her own terms, or wait for the market to adjust. Each has costs, risks and people affected by it. No analysis tells her which risk her company should accept.

Domain knowledge made the whole sequence possible. Anita noticed the missing customer segment because she knew her region, and that, to my mind, is why knowing things still matters when facts are easy to retrieve: knowledge is what lets you see that something is missing, implausible or out of context. Implementation expertise matters for the same reason: knowing how distributors actually respond to a change in terms is not something an analysis can fully supply.
The three-question diagnostic
The framework becomes useful when you turn it into questions you ask about your own work:
Can I verify the facts?
Do I know which claims are material, and have I checked them?
Can I explain the reasoning?
Could I describe why this conclusion follows, and what else might explain the same evidence?
Can I justify and own the decision?
Could I defend the choice, including what it sacrifices, to someone affected by it?
These questions matter more as the stakes rise. That is an argument for scrutinising what comes back, and only rarely for using less AI on important work.
Producing an answer versus being able to defend it

There is early evidence that assisted performance and independent capability can diverge. Bastani and colleagues (2025) ran a field experiment with high-school mathematics students in Turkey. Students given access to a general-purpose AI assistant during practice performed better on practice problems. When access was removed for an exam, they did worse than students who had practised without it, by about 17 per cent on the authors' measure. A version of the assistant designed to give hints rather than answers largely avoided that loss.

This is one study of students doing mathematics, not professionals doing their jobs, and it does not show long-term decline. A different kind of evidence comes from Lee and colleagues (2025), who surveyed 319 knowledge workers about 936 real uses of generative AI. Workers who reported higher confidence in AI tended to report applying less critical thinking; those with more confidence in their own abilities reported applying more. This is self-reported association, not proof of cause.
Neither study settles the question, but together they point to something this book keeps returning to: technology can expand

what a professional produces without expanding what that professional understands. Better output is valuable, and nothing here argues against it. What the studies suggest is that output and understanding can come apart, and that the difference may only show when the assistance is taken away. Access to assistance can be bought; the capability to use it well has to be built by the person who will rely on it.
Exercise: audit one AI-assisted decision
Choose a recent decision or piece of work where you used AI. On one page, write four short sections:
Verified facts:
the material facts, and how you know each is true.
Causal explanation:
why you believe the situation is as it is, plus at least one alternative explanation.
Chosen action:
what you decided or recommended.
Trade-offs:
what the choice gives up, and who bears the cost.
Mark every point you could not write without going back to the AI output. Then identify one verification step you could take this week to close the most important gap.
Reflection:
Could I explain this decision to a colleague without the AI output in front of me?

If the honest answer is “not yet”, you have learned something useful. Where the time to close that gap might come from is another question, and part of the answer may already be sitting in the hours AI saves you.

sections.label: Chapter 2 — Reclaiming Your Intellectual Potential
sections.title: Reclaiming Your Intellectual Potential

runs.text: In Plato's
Phaedrus

, Socrates tells a story about the invention of writing. The god Theuth presents it to King Thamus as a gift that will make people wiser. Thamus is unconvinced. With writing, he says, people “will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing” (Plato, trans. Jowett).

Thamus was half right. Writing did change memory, and it also made possible libraries, science and this book. What I take from the story is less a warning about decline than a reminder of choice: every powerful tool for thought arrives with a decision about what we let it do for us and what we keep doing ourselves. Generative AI presents that old decision more often, and across more kinds of work, than earlier tools did.

Karthik is a compliance analyst at a bank in Chennai. Much of his week used to go into drafting routine documents: policy summaries, audit responses, standard letters to business units. With an AI assistant he now produces first drafts in a fraction of the time. His manager noticed. Within two months Karthik was handling the workload of a colleague who had moved to another team.

As stories go, this is a good one. Karthik is more productive, his team is better served and his manager has reason to value him. But consider a feasible alternative. Suppose he had kept back two hours a week, a small share of what he saved, to understand the regulations behind the documents he drafts: why a rule exists, how regulators have interpreted it, where it conflicts with others. In a year he would be producing the same volume of work and would also be the person his team turns to when a question has no template.
Neither path is wrong. What strikes me is how rarely anyone chooses between them deliberately.
What offloading is, and what it costs
Psychologists use the term
cognitive offloading

for actions that reduce the mental demands of a task, such as writing a reminder, setting an alarm or tilting your head to read rotated text (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). Offloading is ordinary and usually sensible. Nobody needs to memorise phone numbers. Freeing working memory from routine detail can leave more room for the parts of a task that matter.

The complication is that some mental effort is how we learn, which makes it more than a cost to be minimised. Research on study techniques consistently finds that effortful methods, such as testing yourself and spacing practice over time, produce more durable learning than easy ones like rereading or highlighting (Dunlosky et al., 2013). Effort spent retrieving and reconstructing knowledge builds the knowledge. When a tool removes that effort, it may also remove the practice.
The useful distinction, then, lies between
offloading that frees you for more valuable thinking
and
delegation that quietly removes practice you still need
, rather than between using AI and avoiding it. Formatting a document is the first kind for nearly everyone. Drafting an argument may be the second kind for someone still learning to argue.

Nor is this only a classroom concern. In four Polish endoscopy centres, researchers compared experienced doctors' colonoscopies performed without AI support before and after an AI detection tool arrived. In the non-AI procedures, the rate of detecting precancerous growths fell from 28.4 to 22.4 per cent (Budzyń et al., 2025). The study was observational, so it cannot prove the tool caused the decline. A 2026 prospective trial in Norway, using a different design and detection measure, found no statistically significant decline after AI was withdrawn (Pedersen et al., 2026), so the question remains open. The Polish result is still a sober reminder that skills we stop exercising may not wait for us.
Headline savings and net savings

The productivity gains from AI can be real. In a controlled experiment, Noy and Zhang (2023) gave 453 college-educated professionals occupation-specific writing tasks. Those with access to ChatGPT took about 40 per cent less time, and their output was rated about 18 per cent higher in quality. These were specific, short writing tasks, not whole jobs, but the result shows how large the effect can be.

Your own savings may be smaller once you count everything. The time to write a prompt, read the output, check its facts, fix its errors and redo work that missed the point all counts. A draft that took ten minutes instead of sixty, plus thirty minutes of checking, saved twenty minutes, not fifty. That number, after review and rework, is your
net saving
. It is the only one worth planning around.

Our sense of what we save can also be wrong. In a 2025 trial by the research group METR, sixteen experienced software developers worked on real tasks from their own projects, with AI allowed on some and not others. They expected AI to speed them up. It slowed them down by about 19 per cent, and afterwards they still believed it had helped (Becker et al., 2025). One small study of one kind of work proves little in general, and METR itself now treats the result as a snapshot of early-2025 tools. In a 2026 update, its researchers said they believe developers are likely more sped up by newer AI tools, while cautioning that their new data offer only weak evidence for this, partly because developers who rely most on AI increasingly declined to take part (Becker et al., 2026). It is a good reason to measure your savings before believing in them.
Three dividends
Every hour AI saves goes somewhere. Broadly, it can become one of three dividends.

rows: More output, more tasks, faster delivery

runs.text: All three are legitimate, and they are less separate than the table suggests. Productive work builds expertise; doing more of a task, with feedback, is one of the oldest ways people get good at things. Rest supports learning too, since tired minds consolidate little and notice less. The difference is that productivity and rest develop capability as a by-product, when the work happens to stretch you and the rest happens to restore you. Intellectual development does it on purpose. If none of your saved time is ever directed that way,
your growth depends on whatever your work and your evenings happen to teach you.

runs.text: Cognitive reinvestment, the deliberate conversion of that dividend into growth, takes four steps:
Identify
your net savings honestly, after review and rework.
Allocate
a realistic portion to learning. Even a small, protected block beats a large, imaginary one.
Invest
it in effortful activity: study, unaided reasoning, reflection and application, rather than more passive reading.
Demonstrate
the learning by using it on a real problem, so you can see whether it changed what you can do.

Each cycle starts from what the last one taught you.

runs.text: Spending five hours learning something is an investment, but the hours alone tell us little about what we have gained. A better measure is whether we can now understand, explain or solve something that previously defeated us. That is the return cognitive
reinvestment aims at, and like any return it can be hoped for but not promised.

I call this a dividend deliberately. Like a financial dividend, it is a return on something you already hold, here the productivity AI gives you, and it can be reinvested or spent. Most discussion of AI and thinking asks how to avoid losing skills. The dividend asks a more ambitious question: what could you build with effort you no longer need to spend?
Where these ideas come from

The ideas in this chapter draw on existing research, and I want to be clear about which parts are borrowed. The capability gap builds on research into cognitive offloading. Risko and Gilbert (2016) treat offloading partly as a question of metacognition: people tend to offload when they believe it is more efficient than relying on their own abilities, and those beliefs are not always accurate. That is one reason cognitive reinvestment starts with an honest measure of what has actually been saved. Reinvestment itself draws on research on deliberate practice, the finding that expert performance grows through prolonged effort at activities designed to improve it (Ericsson et al., 1993). That finding came from musicians' retrospective estimates of their own practice, and a later replication, discussed below, suggests that practice explains less of the difference between performers than was first reported. In a recent review of AI-supported STEM learning, the education researcher Daiki Nakamura (2026) proposes what he calls offloading regulation, the competence to decide which cognitive work to hand to AI and which to keep. The five-stage method in Chapter 9 borrows from studies of human–AI collaboration, which suggest that how people work with AI matters as much as whether they use it (Dell'Acqua et al., 2026; Shen & Tamkin, 2026).

What I hope is distinctive is the combination: treating the efficiency AI provides as a resource that working professionals can deliberately convert into their own development, outside any classroom and without anyone designing the curriculum for them.

There are honest limits here. Not everyone controls their saved time. In many workplaces faster work simply means more work, and nobody can announce that two hours a week now belong to personal development. Then the dividend may be smaller, or may have to be found inside the work itself: drafting one section unaided, say, or spending ten minutes understanding a rule instead of just applying it. Nor is there any duty to reinvest every saved minute. My claim is narrower than it may first appear. Saved effort becomes an
opportunity only for someone who is able, and decides, to put it to work.
Two ways to spend the same five hours

Consider two professionals in the same role, both hypothetical. After checking and rework, AI tools save each of them about five hours a week. Over a working year of 48 weeks that comes to 240 hours each, roughly six working weeks. The figures are illustrative.
Professional A puts all 240 hours into additional work: more reports, more clients, faster turnaround. Her output rises, and so, quite reasonably, does her manager's opinion of her.

Professional B splits the same time. About two hours a week, 96 hours over the year, go to additional work. The other three hours a week, 144 hours in all, go to deliberate intellectual practice. She studies a field next to her own, perhaps the economics of the industry her clients work in. She reasons through some problems before consulting AI, then compares her answer with its answer. She examines the assumptions behind her team's standard methods, and she writes short notes explaining what she has understood.

runs.text: Is B better off at the end of the year? Not necessarily. A has produced more, and in many organisations that is what gets noticed. B's practice might have been unfocused or aimed at the wrong subjects. What I claim is more modest. B has created conditions in which lasting capability can grow, and A has not, unless A's additional work happened to stretch her. Research on learning and expertise describes those conditions fairly consistently: effortful rather than passive activity (Dunlosky et al., 2013), practice aimed at improving performance rather than repeating it (Ericsson et al., 1993), application to real problems, and some form of feedback. Without them, 144 hours can be spent as unproductively as any others. We will meet both professionals again in Chapter 10.
Six objections worth taking seriously
An argument is only as good as its answers to the best case against it. These are the six objections I find strongest.
“AI itself improves thinking.”

Sometimes it does. In experiments by Lira and colleagues (2026), people who practised writing cover letters with an AI tool later wrote better ones without it, apparently because the AI's revisions worked as tailored examples. In the customer-support study in Chapter 6, less experienced agents seemed to learn from the assistant. I do not claim that using AI weakens thinking. I claim that its effect depends on how it is used, and that the difference is worth managing deliberately. The study involved one kind of writing, and it would be a mistake to generalise from it too quickly. Cognitive reinvestment includes using AI as a coach. It excludes only using it as a substitute for the effort that learning requires.
“Offloading is natural. Why treat AI differently?”

We have always offloaded memory to writing, arithmetic to calculators and navigation to maps, and mostly we were right to. The difference is one of reach. Earlier tools took over well-defined operations. AI can take over drafting, explanation, analysis and recommendation, which are the very activities through which understanding and judgment are built. A calculator that does your sums still leaves you to decide which sums are worth doing. A tool that also drafts, argues and recommends leaves much less, unless you keep some of that work for yourself. None of this means holding on to every skill that technology makes unnecessary. The challenge is to tell the skills we can safely relinquish from the capabilities we need to keep in order to understand, evaluate and direct the systems we increasingly depend on.
“Specialisation creates value. Why learn what a machine can do?”

Division of labour is one of the great engines of prosperity, and nobody needs to master everything their tools can do. But specialisation has always relied on someone who understands enough to direct and check the specialist. When the specialist is a machine that sounds equally confident when it is right and when it is wrong, that supervising understanding is worth more, not less. Chapter 5 returns to this point.
“The time saved belongs to my employer.”

Often it does, and I have tried not to pretend otherwise. Where that is so, the dividend shrinks to the small practices later in this chapter, which fit inside the work. Organisations have their own reasons to share it, since they depend on people who can catch the errors AI makes, and Chapter 1 suggests that capacity cannot be taken for granted. But no reader should have to win that argument before beginning.
“AI may judge better than I do. Why not delegate?”

For some tasks it will, and for some it already does. Delegating those is sensible. Even then, someone has to decide which tasks they are, notice when conditions change and answer for the outcome, and all three require enough understanding to evaluate a judgment you did not make yourself. Chapter 9 offers a working rule for when delegation is reasonable.
“Effort doesn't guarantee improvement.”

True, and this may be the most important objection of the six. Hours alone make nobody better. When Macnamara and Maitra (2019) repeated the classic study of violinists on which much deliberate-practice research rests, accumulated practice still mattered, but it explained considerably less of the difference in skill than the original study had reported, and it did not separate the best players from the good ones. As far as the evidence goes, what makes practice productive is its design: effortful retrieval rather than rereading, a clear target, feedback and application to real problems. That is why cognitive reinvestment ends with demonstration instead of hours logged, and why every exercise in this book asks for an output you can inspect.
When there is no time to protect

For many readers, that paragraph understates the problem. Picture a test lead at an IT services firm, three weeks from go-live on a fixed-price project, every hour already committed. Whatever AI saves her disappears into the backlog before she notices it existed. Telling her to reserve two hours a week would only remind her of what she cannot do.
If that is your situation, take the dividend in small amounts inside the work itself. Each of these takes minutes:
Predict before you prompt.
Write one line on what you expect the answer to be, then compare.
Explain one claim.
Pick the most important claim in an AI output and explain, without looking, why it is true.
Write one part yourself.
In a document you would normally delegate entirely, draft one paragraph first.
Ask one “why”.
When applying a rule or template, find out once why it exists.
Close the day.
Write one sentence on something you understood today that you did not yesterday.

These practices will not transform anyone in a week. They keep independent thinking alive through periods when nothing more is possible, and make it easier to do more when pressure eases. Every exercise in this book can be scaled down the same way.
Exercise: a seven-day dividend log
For seven working days, keep a simple log of tasks where you used AI. For each, record five things:
The task.
Your estimate of how long it would have taken without AI.
Time actually spent with AI.
Time spent checking and reworking.
Net saving (item 2 minus items 3 and 4).

At the end of the week, total your net savings. Reserve a feasible block from them, even thirty minutes, for one learning activity connected to your work. Then demonstrate it: apply what you learned to a real task and note what you did differently.
Reflection:
Which task should I keep practising without AI, because doing it myself is how I stay good at it?

sections.title: Developing Your Thinking Capabilities

sections.label: Chapter 3 — Think for Yourself
sections.title: Think for Yourself

runs.text: In 2023 two New York lawyers filed a court submission in a personal-injury case against the airline Avianca. It cited several court decisions supporting their client. The airline's lawyers could not find them, and neither could the judge, because they did not exist. ChatGPT had invented them, complete with quotations and citations, and the lawyer who did the research had relied on the tool's assurances about its sources. The court sanctioned the lawyers and their firm, noting that they had continued to stand by the fake opinions after their existence was questioned (
Mata v. Avianca, Inc.

It is tempting to read this as a story about careless use of technology. I think it is better read as a story about belief. A fluent, confident, well-formatted answer arrived, and it was believed. He had plenty of information. What he lacked was the habit of asking how he knew.

The same habit matters in ordinary offices. A software project at a logistics company is three months late. In the steering meeting, the explanation forms quickly. The vendor's team is weak, the developers missed estimates and the project manager did not push hard enough. Everyone in the room has seen projects fail for these reasons. Within twenty minutes the discussion has moved to replacing the vendor.

One member of the group, a business analyst named Fatima, asks for a day before the decision. She pulls the change log. Over the three months, the business side has submitted forty-one change requests, and the scope has grown by roughly a third. (The figures here are illustrative.) Execution may still be part of the problem. But a team building a moving target will look slow no matter who it is.
Fatima was not being contrary. She did something more useful, and rarer: she treated an explanation everyone shared as a hypothesis, and checked it.
Where our beliefs come from

Most of what any of us believes, we did not work out ourselves. We absorbed it from teachers, colleagues, industry wisdom and experience that was never examined closely. That is unavoidable; nobody can verify everything. The trouble starts when inherited beliefs feel like conclusions we reached.
Two well-documented tendencies make this worse.
Confirmation bias
is the tendency to seek, interpret and remember evidence in ways that support what we already believe (Nickerson, 1998).
Motivated reasoning

is the tendency for our goals, including the wish to be right or to protect our group, to shape which conclusions we find convincing (Kunda, 1990). Neither means people reason badly all the time. They mean that, left unchecked, reasoning tends to drift toward comfortable answers.
In the steering meeting, “the vendor is weak” was comfortable. It located the problem outside the business team, and it matched familiar stories.
When the explanation arrives ready-made

AI adds something new to these old tendencies. Confirmation bias describes how we treat evidence for beliefs we already hold. Increasingly, though, beliefs arrive already formed: a fluent explanation, delivered in seconds, before we have thought about the question at all. I suspect this matters more than any single bias. A ready-made explanation becomes the first draft of our view, and later evidence gets measured against it.

Fluency makes this hard to notice, because a well-written answer feels well-reasoned whether or not it is. In the survey by Lee and colleagues (2025), knowledge workers who reported more confidence in AI also reported less critical thinking about its output. Self-reports cannot establish cause. But the pattern fits the Avianca case: the risk that concerns me most is less that AI hands us wrong beliefs than that it hands us beliefs we never quite chose.
The defence is simple to state. Before you ask, decide what you currently think, however roughly. The answer then becomes evidence about your view rather than a replacement for it.
Evidence and interpretation

A useful habit is to separate what was observed from what it is taken to mean. “The project is three months late” is evidence. “The developers are slow” is an interpretation. So is “the scope kept changing”, until someone checks the change log.
Once you see interpretations as interpretations, three practices follow.
Look for disconfirming evidence.
Ask what you would expect to see if your explanation were wrong, then look for it. If the vendor were weak, its other projects should also be struggling. Are they?
Generate alternatives.

Before settling on an explanation, list at least two others that fit the same evidence. Changing requirements, unclear ownership and an unrealistic original estimate could each produce the same delay.
Calibrate and revise.
Hold conclusions with confidence proportional to the evidence. Say “probably” when you mean probably. When new evidence arrives, adjust, and notice how hard that feels.
Julia Galef (2021) describes the underlying attitude as a
scout mindset

: the motivation to see things as they are rather than to defend a position. In her account, the soldier asks “Can I believe it?” of claims they like and “Must I believe it?” of claims they dislike. The scout asks, “Is it true?”
A word on intuition

Gut feeling deserves a fairer hearing than it often gets in books like this. Kahneman and Klein (2009) found common ground on when intuition deserves trust: when a person has long practice in an environment regular enough to learn from, with timely feedback. An experienced nurse or a seasoned plant engineer often senses a problem before they can explain it. The right response is to treat that sense as a strong hypothesis worth investigating, not as proof, and not as noise.
Independence is responsiveness to reasons

Independence, then, has little to do with contrarianism. Your conclusions are independent when they respond to reasons, whether or not they happen to differ from the consensus. Someone who always disagrees is no more independent than someone who always agrees; both are following a rule instead of the evidence. Fatima might have concluded that the vendor really was the problem, and her thinking would have been just as independent. Nor does independent thinking guarantee better decisions. What it does guarantee is that your errors are your own, and so you can find and correct them.
This is also what separates knowledge from confident assertion. In the practical sense this book uses, a belief earns the name when you can say what supports it and what would count against it.

Can independent thinking be learned? There is reasonable evidence that it can be taught. A large review of critical-thinking instruction found a modest positive average effect, with the strongest results when teaching included discussion, work on authentic problems and mentoring (Abrami et al., 2015). Those are conditions you can
create for yourself: argue with colleagues, practise on real decisions and seek out people who reason well.
Used in the right order, AI is a good sparring partner. Ask it for the strongest case against your view after you have formed one. Before that, it is simply another confident voice to agree with.
Exercise: put one belief on trial
Choose a belief you hold about your work: a cause you are sure of, a practice you consider best, a judgment about a person or team. Write:
The belief, in one sentence.
The evidence that supports it.
The strongest counterargument you can construct.
What evidence would change your mind.
Your confidence before and after this exercise, as a rough percentage.
If your confidence did not move at all, check whether step 3 was as strong as you could make it.
Reflection:
Am I defending this conclusion, or investigating it?
Testing a belief, though, assumes you are working on the right problem, and that is not always so.

sections.label: Chapter 4 — Ask Questions That Change the Problem
sections.title: Ask Questions That Change the Problem

runs.text: When answers become cheap, what becomes expensive? I think the answer is questions. An AI assistant will answer almost anything you ask, quickly and fluently. It will rarely tell you that you asked the wrong thing. As the cost of producing answers falls towards zero, the value of choosing the right problem rises, because a well-made answer to the wrong question now arrives faster and looks more convincing than ever.

The customer-support team at an online insurance company has a clear target: close tickets faster. Average resolution time has become the headline number in every monthly review. The team responds well. Agents use templates, escalate less and close tickets as soon as a reply is sent. Resolution time falls steadily.

Meanwhile, something else rises. The same customers keep coming back with the same problems. Repeat contacts climb month after month. Nobody is doing anything wrong. The team is answering the question it was given:
how do we close tickets faster?
The trouble is that the question was never the right one.
What the original question hides

Every question carries assumptions. “How do we close tickets faster?” assumes that slow closure is the problem, that a closed ticket is a solved problem and that speed is what customers value most. Each assumption may be partly true. Each also hides something. Under that framing, a ticket closed quickly and reopened next week counts as two successes.

The first step in better questioning is to write the original question down and ask what it takes for granted. This is less obvious than it sounds. Questions arrive pre-packaged in targets, dashboards and meeting agendas, and they feel like facts about the situation rather than choices someone made.
Symptoms and causes

The second step is to separate what has been measured from what has been assumed. Resolution time is a measured symptom. So is the rise in repeat contacts. “Agents are too slow” is an untested cause. So is “customers are confused by the policy wording”, or “the claims system gives agents incomplete information.”

This distinction matters because measurements tend to become targets, and a target can be met in ways that leave the underlying problem untouched. When people are rewarded for improving a number, they often find the cheapest route to the number. Nobody need be dishonest for this to happen; it is a reasonable response to the incentive. But it means the number can improve while the situation gets worse.
Reframing the problem
The third step is to identify constraints and then define the problem in ways that point somewhere different. For the support team, three possibilities:
A speed problem:
“How do we resolve issues faster without increasing repeat contacts?” This keeps speed but adds a guard against gaming it.
A resolution problem:
“Why do certain issues recur, and what would resolve them the first time?” This shifts attention from the agent's reply to the customer's outcome.
A demand problem:
“Why do customers need to contact us at all for these issues?” This looks upstream, at policy documents, claims processes and website design.

They may look like three phrasings of one question. In fact each points to different evidence, different owners and different solutions. The first leads to agent training. The second to a study of recurring issues. The third might lead to rewriting a policy document and never involve the support team at all.
The last step is to choose a framing you can actually investigate. A good working question is specific enough that some evidence could answer it, at least partly.

Reframing does not assume every problem has a single root cause. Many problems have several contributing causes, and different framings may each capture part of the truth. The aim is simply to avoid being trapped inside the first question you were handed.
Why framing comes first

A better answer to the wrong question does not help much. A faster ticket-closure process, however elegant, will not fix a confusing claims form. And the better our tools become at producing answers, the more of our own effort belongs upstream, in deciding what is worth answering.

There is research suggesting that the way people find and define problems matters. In a well-known study of art students, Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi (1976) observed that students who spent more time exploring and defining what to draw tended to produce work that judges rated as more original. That was one setting, with artists rather than managers, and it should not be stretched too far. But it fits a broader point in the systems literature: the structure of a situation, including how it is defined and measured, shapes the behaviour it produces (Meadows, 2008).

Framing is where understanding begins. The question you ask controls which evidence you seek, and so which explanations you are ever in a position to test. A team that asks only about closure speed will never collect the evidence that would point to a confusing claims form.
Where AI fits

AI is useful for generating alternative framings. Ask it to restate a problem from the customer's view, the regulator's view or the finance team's view, and you will usually get options you had not considered. The order matters, though. Write down your original framing and its assumptions first. Otherwise you may simply swap one unexamined frame for another, this time supplied by a machine.

There is a subtler risk. AI systems answer the question as it is posed. The more capable they become, the more thoroughly they will solve whatever problem you hand them, including the wrong one. That is one reason I suspect problem formulation will become more valuable as AI improves, though this is a judgment rather than a research finding. It is also a capability that develops only through practice on real problems, which is what the exercise below asks for.
Exercise: three framings
Take a real problem you are working on. Write:
The original question, as it was given to you.
Three materially different framings of the problem.
For each framing, one testable prediction: if this framing is right, what should we observe?
One evidence check that would help discriminate between the framings.
Reflection:
What did the original question make invisible?

sections.label: Chapter 5 — See Connections Others Miss
sections.title: See Connections Others Miss

runs.text: Ask an AI assistant what a legal team's backlog has in common with a factory, a hospital emergency department or a restaurant kitchen, and within seconds you will have a confident list. A few items will be illuminating. Others will be word associations dressed up as ideas. Producing connections has become effortless. Judging which of them mean anything has not.

Consider a hypothetical case. The in-house legal team at a growing technology firm reviews every customer contract before signature. The team is capable and works hard, yet the sales department complains constantly about waiting. The legal head's instinct is to ask for two more lawyers.

A new team member, who once worked in manufacturing operations, sees the problem differently. To her, the legal team looks like a factory floor with too much work in progress. Every lawyer has fifteen or twenty contracts open at once, each partly reviewed, each waiting for something. She remembers a result from queueing theory called
Little's Law

(Little, 1961). In a stable system, the average number of items in the system equals the rate at which items arrive multiplied by the average time each item spends inside. Rearranged, it says something useful: if the team's throughput stays the same, the more contracts that are open at once, the longer each one takes.

Instead of hiring, she proposes to limit how many contracts each lawyer has open, finish before starting, and send simple contracts down a faster lane. Whether this works is an empirical question. But it is a different idea, and it came from another field. I find something quietly delightful in that: a theorem about queues, proved in 1961, has something useful to say about a legal department.
Depth and breadth

The idea worked in her head because she had two things: depth in operations, enough to know what Little's Law actually says, and enough familiarity with legal work to see where it might apply. Learning across disciplines becomes useful when we understand those disciplines well enough to recognise which ideas transfer to other problems and which do not.
David Epstein (2019) argues in
Range

that breadth of experience is especially valuable in what researchers call “wicked” learning environments, where rules are unclear, feedback is delayed and patterns do not simply repeat. Much professional work fits that description. Epstein does not claim that generalists always beat specialists, and neither does this chapter. In stable domains with fast, accurate feedback, deep specialised practice remains hard to beat.

None of this is an argument against specialisation. A specialist who works with AI needs two things that the tool cannot supply: enough breadth to see where a borrowed idea might apply, and enough depth to tell when the machine's confident suggestion is wrong. Without depth, breadth tends to produce clever metaphors. Without breadth, a specialist is left with whatever connections the tool happens to offer.
Structure, not surface
What makes an analogy useful? The cognitive scientist Dedre Gentner (1983) proposed that good analogies map
relationships

, not surface features. A contract is nothing like a car part. What carries across is the relationship between work in progress, throughput and waiting time. Gentner's structure-mapping theory also holds that analogies are stronger when they carry a connected system of relationships rather than isolated similarities.

The difficulty is that people rarely notice structural parallels on their own. In classic experiments, Gick and Holyoak (1980) gave participants a story whose solution could be applied to a later problem. Many failed to use it until they were given a hint that the story was relevant. Transfer across domains is possible, but it does not happen automatically. That is why looking for connections deliberately is a skill worth practising, and one that anyone can improve.
Associations and connections

Whatever else they are, large language models are remarkably good at association. They have absorbed patterns linking words and ideas across an enormous range of text, which makes them useful for suggesting where an analogy might be found. It does not make every suggestion a connection in Gentner's sense. An association says two things are often mentioned together, or sound alike. A connection says the same relationships hold in both, so the same consequences should follow. Only the second can be tested, and only someone who understands at least one of the domains well can test it.

This shifts part of the human contribution. Suggesting a possible connection has become cheap, so more of the value now lies in telling a structural parallel from a pleasing coincidence and working out what the parallel predicts. My working rule is that AI can widen the search, while the validation stays with someone who knows how the domains actually behave.
Testing the analogy

A useful analogy also tells you where it fails. Contracts are not identical parts. Some take an hour; some take a month. Some are blocked by the customer, not by the lawyer. Little's Law describes long-run averages in a reasonably stable system, so it says little about one urgent contract. And lawyers, unlike machines, may lose time switching between many open matters, which strengthens the case for limiting work in progress but is a separate effect from the one the law describes.

runs.text: So the operations analyst should not claim the analogy proves anything. She should use it to make a prediction: if the team limits open contracts, average turnaround should fall without extra staff. Then run a small test, perhaps with one lawyer or one contract type for a month, and look at the result.

That, I think, is the proper partnership between an outside idea and domain expertise. The outside concept supplies a hypothesis; the insider knows where it fits, where it breaks and how to test it without doing harm. Breadth earns its keep when the connections it suggests can be tested and rest on real depth somewhere, and at its
best it lets you explain a familiar situation with tools borrowed from an unfamiliar one.
Building breadth deliberately

Breadth needs a habit more than a second degree. A practical approach is to read regularly in one field adjacent to your own and one field far from it, choosing explanations of core ideas over news. For a finance professional, adjacent might be operations; distant might be ecology or history. When you meet a concept, ask what relationship it describes and where else that relationship might appear.

AI is a useful companion here. It can explain an unfamiliar concept at your level, suggest where else it has been applied and point out its known limits. Its suggestions are starting points. Check the concept in a reliable source before you build on it, because a confident wrong explanation of an outside idea is hard for a non-expert to spot.
Exercise: map an analogy
Choose one concept from a field outside your own. Then:
Describe the concept in two sentences, in your own words.
Map its key relationships onto a problem at work. Which element corresponds to which?
Specify at least two places where the analogy fails.
Propose one small, low-risk test that would tell you whether the borrowed idea helps.
Reflection:
What evidence would distinguish a useful analogy from a clever metaphor?

sections.label: Chapter 6 — See the System, Not Just the Problem
sections.title: See the System, Not Just the Problem

runs.text: Organisations adopting AI are, in effect, running many small productivity experiments at once. A team drafts proposals in half the time. A developer writes code faster. A support desk answers routine questions automatically. Each improvement is real, and each is measured locally, by the people who benefit from it. Far fewer people measure what happens downstream. The gap between local gains and system-wide effects is easy to miss, and the problem behind it is much older than AI.

A product team at a fintech company starts missing delivery dates. Senior leadership, reasonably worried, asks for more visibility: a weekly status report, then a daily stand-up with stakeholders, then a dashboard updated twice a week. Each request makes sense on its own.

Three months later the team spends close to a day a week on reporting. (The figure is illustrative.) Less time goes into building, so dates slip further. Leadership, more worried, asks for still closer tracking. Nobody in this story is foolish or acting in bad faith. Each person is responding sensibly to what they can see. Together, they have built a machine for producing delays.
Complicated and complex
A loose distinction between two kinds of situation is useful here. A
complicated
situation has many parts, but they relate in stable, knowable ways. A jet engine is complicated; an expert can trace how a fault in one part affects another. A
complex

situation has parts that adapt to one another, so behaviour emerges from their interaction and is hard to predict from any single part. A market, a city's traffic and an organisation are complex in this sense.

The line between the two is not sharp, and most real situations mix both. But the distinction matters because complicated problems often yield to analysis of the parts, while complex ones require attention to relationships. The delivery delays were not located in any one person. They
emerged
from how reporting, capacity and worry fed into one another.
Feedback, delays and unintended consequences

Donella Meadows (2008) offers a compact vocabulary for this. A system has stocks, things that accumulate, such as backlog, trust or skill, and flows that change them. Its behaviour is shaped by feedback loops.
A
reinforcing loop
amplifies change in the same direction. More delays lead to more reporting, which leaves less time for delivery, which leads to more delays. Reinforcing loops produce spirals, upward or downward.
A
balancing loop
pushes a system toward a goal or limit. When a backlog grows, a manager may assign more people to it until it shrinks. Balancing loops produce stability, or resistance to change.

runs.text: Most systems contain both, and which one dominates can shift over time.
Delays

make all of this harder. The effects of a decision often show up weeks or months later, by which time people have already reacted again. Delays are why well-meant interventions overshoot, and why the consequences of a decision are so often blamed on something else.
One result is the
unintended consequence

: an action that achieves its immediate aim while producing a side effect elsewhere. The online insurer from Chapter 4 offers a second example. Suppose it automates routine support queries with an AI assistant. Costs fall and simple queries are answered instantly, as intended. But junior agents used to learn the business by handling those simple queries.

Over a year or two, the pipeline of experienced agents able to handle difficult cases may thin out. Nothing in the first month's dashboard would show this. We will return to that insurer in later chapters.
When local gains become system costs

AI makes this pattern more likely for a simple reason: it speeds up the production of work much more than the review of work. If drafting a report becomes five times faster but reading it does not, the volume of reports can grow until reviewers are overwhelmed, and the organisation may decide more slowly than before. Faster code can mean more code to test. Faster proposals can mean more proposals to evaluate. The METR developers in Chapter 2 hint at how time saved in one step can be lost in another.

Sometimes the gain and the risk sit in the same result. Studying more than five thousand customer-support agents, Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (2025) found that an AI assistant raised the number of customer issues resolved per hour by about 15 per cent on average. The gains were concentrated among less experienced and lower-skilled agents; the most experienced saw small gains in speed and small declines in quality. The authors suggest the assistant spread the practices of the most able agents, and they also found signs that agents learned from it. That is an encouraging result. It still raises a question no single quarter's data can answer: if the tool carries much of the expertise, how will the next generation of experts be formed, and who will notice when the tool is wrong?
These are plausible mechanisms, not demonstrated outcomes. Systems thinking asks about them before they show up in the numbers, when changing course is still cheap.
Leverage points
Where should you intervene? Meadows describes
leverage points

: places in a system where a small change can produce a large shift. Her central observation is that the most obvious levers, such as adjusting numbers like budgets, taxes and standards, are usually the weakest. Changing the structure of feedback, who has access to what information, the rules of the system or its goals tends to have more effect, and is usually harder.
Here is how four kinds of intervention would play out in the fintech team, from weakest to strongest.
Change a number.
Move the status report from weekly to fortnightly. Reporting falls a little, but the loop is untouched. The next missed date brings the next request, and the load creeps back.
Change an information flow.

Give leadership direct access to the team's live work board, so they can see progress and blockers without asking. Their worry can now be answered without taking time from delivery. This cuts the link that made the loop reinforcing.
Change a rule.
Agree that every new reporting request states what it will cost in delivery time before it is accepted. A cost that was invisible becomes part of the decision.
Change the goal.

Shift the shared aim from “keep leadership informed about delays” to “remove what causes delays.” Leaders start asking “what is blocking you?” instead of “where are you?”, and their attention becomes help rather than a drain.

The stronger interventions are also harder. Changing a report's frequency takes one email. Changing a goal asks leaders to trust a team that has been missing dates, which is exactly what they find difficult. And because of delays, even a good intervention may take weeks to show results. A practical safeguard is to agree in advance how long to observe before judging, so the old loop does not restart after the first bad week.
Why good people get stuck

Sensible individual actions can add up to an outcome nobody wants. When a problem persists despite effort and goodwill, it is worth asking which relationships keep reproducing it. Not every stubborn problem is quietly working as someone designed it; some persist because they are hard, or because nobody has the resources to fix them. But structure is a common and often overlooked explanation, and AI-driven productivity is adding new structure to many organisations, usually faster than anyone maps it.
In practice this means adding a second question to the familiar one. Alongside “who caused this?”, ask “what keeps causing this?”

AI can help draft a map of actors and relationships, and it is good at suggesting side effects you had not considered. It cannot tell you which relationships actually operate in your organisation. That knowledge comes from observation, conversation and the kind of domain depth Chapter 1 described.
Exercise: map one loop
Choose a recurring problem at work, one that keeps returning despite attempts to fix it. Then:
List the main actors involved.
For each, note the incentive or pressure shaping their behaviour.
Draw arrows showing how one actor's behaviour affects another. Mark each arrow + (more leads to more) or – (more leads to less).
Find at least one closed loop. Is it reinforcing or balancing?
Propose one intervention, and predict one side effect it might produce.
Reflection:
Which relationship matters more here than any individual's action?

sections.label: Chapter 7 — Make Better Decisions Without Knowing Everything
sections.title: Make Better Decisions Without Knowing Everything

runs.text: In 2023, researchers working with Boston Consulting Group gave 758 of its consultants realistic tasks, some with access to GPT-4 and some without. On tasks inside what the researchers called AI's “jagged frontier”, consultants using AI did markedly better and faster. On one task deliberately designed to fall outside it, a business problem that required combining spreadsheet data with interview evidence, the result reversed. Consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to reach the correct answer, even though AI made their responses more persuasive and coherent (Dell'Acqua et al., 2026).

That last detail is the one I keep coming back to: the analysis became more polished while becoming less accurate. Under uncertainty, an obviously wrong answer is often less dangerous than a sophisticated one that makes the uncertainty feel smaller than it is.

Vikram runs international expansion for a Hyderabad company that sells accounting software to small businesses. A distributor in a Southeast Asian country is offering an exclusive three-year partnership. The terms are attractive, but the offer expires in six weeks. Reliable data on how many small businesses there would pay for cloud accounting software does not exist. The government's digital-tax rules, which could drive demand sharply, are expected but not yet published.

Vikram's board wants a recommendation. His team has produced a market model with a demand forecast to two decimal places. He knows the precision is an illusion. He also knows that “we don't know enough” is not a recommendation. I have some sympathy for him. Most of the decisions that matter look more like his than like the tidy problems in textbooks.
Risk and uncertainty
The economist Frank Knight (1921) drew a distinction that still helps.
Risk
describes situations where the possible outcomes and their probabilities can be reasonably estimated, like the chance of a component failing, based on thousands of past components.
Uncertainty
describes situations where we cannot confidently list the outcomes, let alone assign them probabilities.
John Kay and Mervyn King (2020) argue that many important decisions in business and policy involve what they call
radical uncertainty
, and that treating such situations as if they were calculable risk leads to false confidence. Their recommended starting question is simple:
What is going on here?
Before modelling anything, build a credible account of the situation.

Vikram's decision mixes both. Some elements are risk-like: the cost of localising the software can be estimated fairly well. Others are uncertain in Knight's sense: whether the tax rules will arrive, and how small businesses will respond.
Asking what is going on

For Vikram, “What is going on here?” breaks into concrete questions no spreadsheet answers. Why is the distributor offering exclusivity now, with a six-week deadline? Perhaps it has lost another software partner and needs a product to sell. Perhaps it has early signals about the tax rules. Each account changes what the deadline means. What happened when similar rules arrived in comparable markets? And where did the forecast's adoption rate come from? When his team traces it, they find it was borrowed from another country and adjusted by judgment. The two decimal places rest on a guess.

These questions do not tell him what to do, but they change what he is asking. “What will demand be?” cannot be answered. “Which choice leaves us in acceptable shape across the futures we can imagine, and able to survive the bad ones?” can. Kay and King describe this as seeking strategies that are robust and resilient rather than optimal for a single forecast.

AI makes the opposite habit easier. A model can now produce a market forecast, a sensitivity table and a confident narrative in minutes, and each looks like evidence. None of them, by itself, reduces the underlying uncertainty; often they organise what was already assumed. Sophistication of analysis and quality of knowledge are different things, and AI has made the first far cheaper than the second. The discipline I would recommend is to ask of any impressive analysis: which of these numbers did someone observe, and which did someone choose?
Working through the three levels
Anita's three levels from Chapter 1 still help, though each now comes with gaps that have to be named.
Knowledge.

What do we actually know? The distributor's track record, the localisation cost, the size of the small-business population from official statistics. What don't we know, and could we find out in six weeks? Perhaps a few conversations with local accountants, who see the market daily.
Understanding.

What explanations compete? One story says demand is latent and the tax rules will unlock it. Another says small businesses will rely on cheaper local tools or on their accountants' software. A third says the market will grow, but slowly, after the partnership has expired. Each story implies different early signals.
Judgment.

Given what we know and don't, what should we do? This is where it is tempting to invent precision. A model can always produce a probability. The question is whether the probability means anything. Use numbers where you have a real basis for them, such as costs, historical rates and comparable launches. Where you don't, say so.
Scenarios, not forecasts
Scenarios are a better tool than forecasts here. A
scenario

is a coherent, plausible story of how the future might unfold. It is not a prediction, and a set of scenarios does not need probabilities attached. Their purpose is to test whether a decision holds up across several futures.

Reversibility and staged commitment

One of the most practical questions in any uncertain decision is how reversible it is. A decision that can be undone cheaply deserves less deliberation than one that cannot. Where possible, convert an irreversible bet into a sequence of smaller, reversible ones.

Vikram might propose a one-year pilot with an option to extend, or a non-exclusive partnership with a smaller upfront investment. The distributor may refuse; then the board faces a clearer choice about the price of commitment. Either way, the staged option buys learning before the largest money is spent.
